explanations.answer: Appeal to him as to a father
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, tells Timothy, his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2), to "…appeal to him as to a father." I think a hard word lands softer when it's handed over with honor. The correction is still on the table, it just comes in gently.

explanations.answer: Let the other elders handle it
explanations.explanation: Paul never mentions passing the job down the hall here. He hands it to Timothy and tells him how: do not rebuke, but appeal. Tossing it to somebody else is like handing off a hot tray of cookies so you don't get burned. Paul wants Timothy holding that tray with the right tone, appealing to him "…as to a father."

explanations.answer: Wait for him to notice himself
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't tell Timothy to sit back and hope. Waiting for somebody to notice on their own is like waiting for the oven to turn itself off. What Paul gives Timothy is an action: "…appeal to him as to a father." The gentle way still means speaking up.
Yes! Paul says, "Treat younger men as brothers…" After the father for the older man, the family picture keeps going. Brothers is the word he picks for the younger men.
That's right. Paul says, "…older women as mothers…" The older man gets a father, and the older women get mothers. Paul is building a whole household for Timothy in a few short lines.

Sons is a fair guess, since Paul just used a father for the older man. But Paul says to treat younger men as brothers, so Timothy stands beside them. Remember, Paul called Timothy his own child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2). That's Paul's relationship with him, not Timothy's with the younger men.
Aunts don't make Paul's list. He names fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters. For the older women, the word is "…mothers…" Same family picture, just a different word.

Daughters would go with the younger women, but Paul doesn't use it. He says, "…and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity." The older women get "mothers." Brothers and sisters are the words for the younger folks.

Paul says the opposite, baker. If a widow has children or grandchildren, "…they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents…" So her family steps in first. The church isn't the first call.

Right, it's false. Paul says a widow's children or grandchildren "…must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents…" The family goes first. Paul adds that this is pleasing in the sight of God.
That's exactly what Paul says. Repaying their parents "…is pleasing in the sight of God." He doesn't say it's a chore or just a duty. God is pleased when a family takes care of its own.

Paul doesn't mention a reward here. He keeps it simpler than that: this is pleasing in the sight of God. I think a lot of us would love a prize for doing the right thing, but the text gives us His delight. That's plenty.

Paul doesn't say that anywhere in this passage. Past sins don't come up in these verses at all. What he says is that repaying parents "…is pleasing in the sight of God." Picture a grown kid who keeps showing up for Mom, week after week, with no trophy and no applause. Paul says God is pleased by that kind of repaying.

Yes, baker. The widow who is truly in need and left all alone "…puts her hope in God…" And Paul says she continues night and day in her petitions and prayers. Her hope sits with God, and her days are full of prayer.

Paul doesn't say neighbors. He says she is left all alone and "…puts her hope in God…" I think being left alone makes that line stand out even more. She continues night and day in her petitions and prayers.

Paul doesn't mention savings at all. He describes her as truly in need and left all alone. A cookie jar of coins isn't the picture. She "…puts her hope in God…" and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers.

explanations.answer: She is dead even while alive
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says: "…she who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is still alive." That's a strong picture, and he puts it right next to the widow who prays night and day. One lives for pleasure and the other puts her hope in God.

explanations.answer: She is free even while alone
explanations.explanation: Paul's words go in a different direction. He says she who lives for pleasure "…is dead even while she is still alive." Free sounds nice, but that isn't the picture he paints. He's showing the opposite of the widow who puts her hope in God.

explanations.answer: She is rich even while in need
explanations.explanation: That's a fun one, kind of like "warm even while frozen." Paul's version is much more serious: she "…is dead even while she is still alive." He's not talking about money at all. He's drawing a line between living for pleasure and hoping in God.

Yes, denied. Paul says, "If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith…" He's saying providing for your family is part of living out what you believe. It's serious, and Paul says it plainly.

Outgrown works for an apron you bought in the wrong size, but not for the faith. Paul's word is "denied." He says anyone who doesn't provide for his own, especially his own household, "…has denied the faith…" Nobody outgrows this one.
Paul turns that around. The word is "denied," not earned. Anyone who does not provide for his own household "…has denied the faith…" Providing for them is part of living it out.

True, and those are Paul's own words. Anyone who does not provide for his own, especially his own household, "…has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever." It's a hard thing to hear. I think Paul says it that strongly because caring for family matters so much.

Paul does say it. Anyone who does not provide for his own, especially his own household, "…has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever." It's heavy, so we take it seriously. The statement is true.

That's it. Paul says, "A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old…" Age is just the first thing on the list. She also needs to be faithful to her husband and well known for good deeds.

Close, but Paul sets the bar higher. He says a widow should be enrolled if she is "…at least sixty years old…" Fifty is a fine number, but it's ten years short of what Paul writes. Sorry, fifty, you almost made the list.
That's a bit higher than Paul goes. His number is sixty: "…at least sixty years old…" Seventy would have waited ten extra years in line. Sixty is the number on the page.
Yes, deeds. Paul says she should be "…well known for good deeds…" Then he lists them, like bringing up children and entertaining strangers. What she's done is what people know her for.
Fortune would be a nice thing to have, but it isn't Paul's word. A widow on this list is "…well known for good deeds…" A pile of money isn't what he's looking for. He's looking at what she's done.

Paul doesn't put health on the list. He says she should be "…well known for good deeds…" Then he gives examples, including washing the feet of the saints. It's about what she has done, not how she's feeling.

explanations.answer: Their passions draw them from Christ
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Paul gives. "For when their passions draw them away from Christ, they will want to marry…" He says that leads to judgment, because they are setting aside their first faith. Paul keeps his eye on their faith.

explanations.answer: They can still find work to support themselves
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't bring up work at all. The reason he gives is that "…their passions draw them away from Christ…" If we add a reason the text doesn't give, we're baking a recipe Paul never wrote.

explanations.answer: The church has no room left on the list
explanations.explanation: Paul never says the list is full. His reason is about the younger widows themselves: "…when their passions draw them away from Christ, they will want to marry…" It's not a space problem. It's a Christ problem.

Paul says something very different. He says they "…will also learn to be idle, going from house to house…" Then he adds that they'd be not only idle, but gossips and busybodies too. Devoting herself to every good work is how he describes the enrolled widow back in verse 10.

That's right, it's false. Paul says they will learn to be idle, "…going from house to house and being not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, discussing things they should not mention." Every good work is how he describes the widows on the list. For these younger ones he warns about idle days.
That's Paul's advice. "So I advise the younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their households…" He says that denies the adversary occasion for slander. Paul gives them a clear path.

explanations.answer: Stay single and serve the church
explanations.explanation: Paul goes the other direction for these younger widows. He says, "…I advise the younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their households…" Serving the church is not what he lays out here. His advice is the household.

Prayer night and day was the picture of the widow truly in need and left all alone (1 Timothy 5:5). For the younger widows, Paul's advice is different: "…marry, have children, and manage their households…" So this one belongs to someone else in the passage.

True. Paul says, "For some have already turned aside to follow Satan." That's a heavy line, and we can let it be heavy. It comes right after he advises the younger widows to marry, have children and manage their households.

Paul does say it, baker: "For some have already turned aside to follow Satan." It's a heavy verse. He says it right after telling the younger widows to marry, have children and manage their households. So the statement is true.
Paul says the opposite. If a believing woman has dependent widows, "…she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened…" The care starts at home. It doesn't get handed to the church.

That's right. Paul says, "If any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened…" She takes care of them herself. Then the church can help the widows who are truly in need.
